edge_899.relationship: Coal and New World resources enabled divergence between comparably developed Eurasian cores (2000)
edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

edge_1050.relationship: Brenner and Isett challenge Pomeranz through social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe’s stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edge_1050.evidence_note: This arrow represents four named interventions, not a verdict of the economic-history entry, which includes Pomeranz and his allies; each establishes something different. Brenner and Isett (JAS 61:2, 2002; online reprint read in part, no folios), on social-property relations: England's divergence came from "this already existing decisive divergence, not England’s capacity to gain access to the American colonies"; the delta followed "a Malthusian pattern", England "a Smithian pattern"; "Contra Pomeranz". Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read by the second research pass), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: "our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England"; "Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism" (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the "rise of the west" literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: "The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers" (p. 958). The qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Robert Brenner is not yet an atlas entry; if he becomes one, his critique with Isett moves to its own arrow.

Later debates concern political action, imperial accumulation, dialectical and analytical explanation, and reproduction of material life.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.
strands.works: Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix and notes17,20

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

dependency.label: Dependency / world-systems
dependency.description: Related but distinct approaches explain development and underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of capitalism, empire, and exchange. Marxist concepts are reworked alongside other resources; dependency theory has non-Marxist as well as Marxist strands, and world-systems analysis is not simply British Marxist social history enlarged. Prebisch’s industrialization strategy, Frank’s metropolitan–satellite hypotheses, dos Santos’s internal/external constraints, Cardoso and Faletto’s political alliances, and Wallerstein’s system-level unit require separate readings. Industrial growth and dependence are not mutually exclusive in all these accounts.

representative_people.context: Proposes that metropolitan–satellite relations historically produce underdevelopment, with hypotheses about export ties and their weakening; this is a contested account, not an earlier national stage.

historicalsociology.label: Comparative historical sociology
historicalsociology.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.

historicalsociology.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Agrarian relations and political routes
strands.focus: Class alliances and rural power produce divergent, often violent paths rather than a smooth democratic sequence.
strands.works: Moore, Social Origins (1966)

strands.title: States and revolutionary transformations
strands.focus: State organizations, agrarian classes and international competition enter a combined explanation.
strands.works: Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979)

strands.title: Contention and repertoires
strands.focus: Historically specific performances link local claims to wider transformations.
strands.works: Tilly, The Contentious French (1986); political-performances essay (1993–1994)

strands.title: Overlapping networks of power
strands.focus: Forms and reach of power are differentiated rather than enclosed in one homogeneous society.
strands.works: Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

strands.title: Comparative Marxian transitions
strands.focus: European transitions and divergent state forms frame a contested comparative synthesis.
strands.works: Anderson, Passages and Lineages (1974)

strands.title: Authority, law and citizenship
strands.focus: Bendix compares authority; Somers examines how local relations and national law shape rights. Their methods are distinct.
strands.works: Bendix (1964); Somers (1993)

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.
strands.works: Block and Somers (1984) on Polanyi (1944)

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.
strands.works: Goldstone, Revolution and Rebellion (1991)

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.
strands.works: Sewell–Skocpol exchange (1985; reprinted 1994)

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.
strands.works: Quest for Excitement (1986)

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.
strands.works: Goldstone (1991), 156–169; Perry review (1992), 827

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. This comparison retains structural-functional and evolutionary assumptions that his retrospective introduction discusses rather than simply disowns.
strands.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces

strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)
